title: Bhikhan's medicine
hookLine: Bhikhan calls the Name the medicine for every illness (Sorath, Bhikhan, ang 659)

cards: The bathroom cabinet. Something for a headache, something for a cough, a half-used tube for a burn, a bottle with a date long gone. Every shelf has a cure for one particular thing.
Bhagat Bhikhan, in Raag Sorath on Ang 659, writes from the other side of all those shelves: an old body, eyes running, voice failing. And he names a single medicine, for every illness.

teach.h: EYES RUNNING, HAIR WHITE AS MILK.
teach.b: He starts with the body, and doesn't flatter it. In paraphrase: water streams from the eyes, the body has grown thin, the hair has turned white as milk. The throat is choked, and the words won't come.
Then the question to himself: what can you do now? It's an honest picture of old age, the kind that's easy to look away from. Then the doctor appears.
In paraphrase: O Lord, my King, be the physician, and save your devotees. He doesn't ask God to stop him aging. He asks for a healer of a different kind.
Then the hymn goes under the skin: the head aches, the body burns, the heart is in pain, a pain no medicine reaches. And he names one.
The Name of the Lord is pure nectar water, the finest medicine in all the world. In the hymn that follows, he calls that Name a jewel beyond price. A medicine is taken regularly, not once.
It works from the inside. It doesn't ask whether you deserve it. That's how Bhikhan speaks of the Name: remembered again and again, working where no ointment reaches.

teach.h: NOT INSTEAD OF A DOCTOR: UNDER THE ACHES.
teach.b: And to be clear about what he isn't saying: the hymn doesn't tell anyone to throw out the cabinet, or to skip the doctor.
Read this way, Bhikhan is talking about the ache underneath the aches: fear, restlessness, the sense of being far from God.
For that, he names one medicine: the Name of the Lord.

how: Bhikhan's hymns are sung in kirtan in Raag Sorath, and Sikh teaching speaks of naam, remembering God's Name, as healing for the mind, alongside ordinary care for the body.

o: a rule to refuse doctors and trust prayer alone
the Lord's Name, for the ache under every ache
a healing herb from an old village garden

games.q: inside the hymns — tap the pairs.
p: eyes running, hair white as milk
what he asks the Lord to be

s: Bhikhan's hymn tells the sick to give up doctors
he asks the Lord to be the physician for the ache under the aches; the hymn says nothing against doctors.
running eyes, a thin body, milk-white hair, a voice that won't come.
Bhikhan asks God to stop him growing old
he asks the Lord to be his physician and save his devotees.

games.q: you're old, your eyes run and your voice fails. what does Bhikhan ask for?
o: that the Lord be his physician.
a stronger medicine from the shelf.
games.why: he asks the Lord, his King, to be the physician, and calls the Name the medicine for every illness.

practice: Find the ache that isn't in a muscle: a worry, a restless loop, a heaviness. Don't fix it; let the breath come and go across it slowly, the way you'd let a medicine work.
If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, a dose taken again and again; if you don't, let the quiet itself be the dose.

wordCard.voice: Bhikhan's medicine. In Raag Sorath, an old devotee asks the Lord to be his physician, and calls the Name the medicine for every illness.

carryVoice: Your line: the name as medicine. Not instead of the doctor, but for the ache underneath. Seven hundred ninety days now.
